questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acceleration of a Particle Given Its Velocity
questions.problem: The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-24t+45.$ Calculate the velocity of the particle when the acceleration $a$ is equal to $0\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-24t+45) \\  & =6t-24\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=0,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6t-24 \\ 6t & =24 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=4,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =3(4)^{2}-24(4)+45 \\  & =48-96+45 \\  & =-3\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=0\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $-3\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+1.$ Calculate the velocity of the particle when the acceleration $a$ is equal to $\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

When $a=\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ the velocity is $v=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=\frac{1}{2},$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{t+1} \\ t+1 & =2 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=1,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)+1 \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1)\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $v=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ is given by $v(t)={t}^{3}{e}^{3t-3},$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Calculate the acceleration of the particle at $t=1$ second.

$a(1)=$
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}{e}^{3t-3}) \\  & =3{t}^{2}{e}^{3t-3}+3{t}^{3}{e}^{3t-3} \\  & =3{t}^{2}(1+t){e}^{3t-3}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration when $t=1$ second, we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =3(1)^{2}(1+1){e}^{3(1)-3} \\  & =3(1)(2){e}^{0} \\  & =6\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)=6{t}^{3}-19{t}^{2}+13,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Find the time when the particle's acceleration is equal to $a=70\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{3}-19{t}^{2}+13) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-38t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(18{t}^{2}-38t) \\  & =36t-38\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=70,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}70 & =36t-38 \\ 36t & =108 \\ t & =3\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the time when the acceleration is $a=70\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $3$ seconds.

$$

$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12{t}^{2}-2t) \\  & =24t-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)={t}^{2}+4\sqrt{t},$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Find the particle's acceleration at $t=1$ second.

$a(1)=$
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4\sqrt{t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+4{t}^{1/2}) \\  & =2t+2{t}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2{t}^{-1/2}) \\  & =2+2(-\frac{1}{2}){t}^{-3/2} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=1$ second, we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =2-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1)^{3}}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem: The position $x$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by $x(t) = 1+2t+3t^2+4t^3$. Calculate the acceleration of the particle at time $t=0$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $x(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t+3{t}^{2}+4{t}^{3}) \\  & =2+6t+12{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+6t+12{t}^{2}) \\  & =6+24t.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=0$, we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(0) & =6+24(0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=0$ is $6$.
